subjects.title: Inference Request Lifecycle
subjects.why: Name stages: tokenize, prefill, decode, detokenize.
subjects.explainer:
Prefill is compute-bound over the full prompt; decode is memory-bound while reading KV. TTFT, ITL/TBT, tokens/s, goodput, queue time, and KV utilization are the dashboard language. Streaming improves perceived latency. Chat templates and tool parsers sit on the critical path — moving render/derender off GPU nodes is an emerging pattern.

Common mistake: maximizing throughput while missing TTFT SLOs. Another: ignoring tokenizer CPU cost on huge batches.

Instrument before you tune.

topics.title: Stages

subtopics.title: Prefill compute-bound
subtopics.text: Prefill multiplies large matrices over all prompt tokens at once, so it keeps GPU compute units busy.

subtopics.title: Decode memory-bound
subtopics.text: Each decode step reads all model weights and the KV cache to produce one token, so memory bandwidth is the limit.

topics.explainer: An inference request passes through clear stages. The server applies the chat template and tokenizes. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel; it is compute-bound and sets time to first token. Decode generates one token per step for every sequence in the batch; it is memory-bandwidth-bound because each step re-reads all weights and the KV cache. Detokenization and tool-call parsing turn ids back into text and structure. Streaming returns tokens as they come; buffering waits for the full output.

topics.title: Metrics

subtopics.title: TTFT / TBT / ITL
subtopics.text: TTFT is time to first token; TBT or ITL is time between later tokens. Users feel TTFT as 'thinking time' and ITL as reading speed.

subtopics.title: Goodput vs throughput
subtopics.text: Goodput is the rate of requests that finished within their latency targets; raw throughput can rise while goodput falls.

subtopics.title: Queue time
subtopics.text: Time spent waiting for a free slot in the engine before prefill starts; it grows quickly near capacity.

topics.explainer: TTFT (time to first token) measures prefill plus queueing. TBT or ITL (time between tokens) measures decode speed per user. Throughput is tokens per second per GPU across all users. Goodput counts only requests that met their SLOs, which is what actually matters. KV cache hit rate shows how much prefix reuse you get. Queue time reveals under-provisioning before latency explodes. Always report percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages.

quiz.why: Full-prompt matmuls dominate.
Every step re-reads weights and KV for little compute.

choices: Only requests that met their latency SLOs
quiz.why: Throughput that violates SLOs is not useful work.

lesson.intuition: Every LLM request goes through the same stages. The prompt is tokenized, the whole prompt is processed in one big parallel pass (prefill), and then the answer is produced one token at a time (decode), each step reading the cached keys and values. Prefill is limited by compute and decode by memory bandwidth, and most serving tricks target one or the other.
how: Tokenize the input and apply the chat template.
Wait in the scheduler queue until the engine has room for the request.
Prefill: process all prompt tokens in parallel, filling the KV cache; this sets time to first token (TTFT).
Decode: generate one token per step, reading all weights and the KV cache each step; this sets time between tokens (TBT or ITL).
Detokenize, parse tool calls or JSON, and stream tokens to the client.
lesson.example: Why decode is memory-bound: an 8B model in bf16 has 16 GB of weights. Each decode step for a single sequence must read all of them. On a GPU with 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth (H100 SXM), that's at least 16 / 3,350 ≈ 4.8 ms per token, at most ≈ 210 tokens per second for one sequence, no matter how many FLOPs are available. Batching many sequences shares that weight read.
mistakes: Reporting only average latency and hiding long-tail TTFT under load.
Measuring throughput without checking whether requests met their SLOs (goodput).
Ignoring queue time, which is often the biggest part of TTFT at peak.
lesson.enterprise: A chat product's p95 TTFT spiked at lunch even though GPU utilization looked fine. Tracing showed queue time made up 70% of TTFT; enabling chunked prefill and adding one replica brought p95 TTFT from 3.1 s back under 1 s.
takeaways: Prefill = compute-bound, decode = memory-bound.
TTFT and TBT are the user-facing metrics.
Goodput counts only requests that met SLOs.

flowchart LR

  Q --> PF[Prefill: all prompt tokens, compute-bound]
  PF --> KV[(KV cache)]
  PF --> D[Decode: 1 token/step, memory-bound]

  DT --> S[Stream to client]

topics.title: Open Engines

subtopics.title: vLLM
subtopics.text: vLLM introduced PagedAttention and offers continuous batching, prefix caching and an OpenAI-compatible server for many model families.

subtopics.title: SGLang
subtopics.text: SGLang adds RadixAttention for prefix reuse and a fast runtime for structured and multi-call programs.

subtopics.title: llama.cpp / Ollama
subtopics.text: llama.cpp runs quantized GGUF models on CPUs, Apple silicon and consumer GPUs; Ollama packages it for easy local use.

topics.explainer: vLLM popularized PagedAttention and continuous batching and supports most models and hardware. SGLang adds RadixAttention for automatic prefix reuse and is strong for structured and agentic workloads. TGI is Hugging Face's server. llama.cpp and Ollama run quantized models on CPUs, Macs and small GPUs. Compare on features you need (quantization formats, speculative decoding, LoRA, structured output, disaggregation) and benchmark on your own traffic shape.

topics.title: NVIDIA Stack

subtopics.title: TensorRT-LLM
subtopics.text: TensorRT-LLM compiles models into optimized engines for NVIDIA GPUs, often with the best raw performance on that hardware.

subtopics.title: NIM
subtopics.text: NVIDIA NIM ships prebuilt inference containers with optimized engines and standard APIs.

topics.explainer: TensorRT-LLM compiles models into optimized engines for NVIDIA GPUs, often the fastest option at the cost of build steps. Triton Inference Server hosts many model types behind one API. NVIDIA Dynamo orchestrates distributed and disaggregated serving with KV-aware routing. NIM packages models as ready-to-run containers. Migrating between stacks costs engineering time, so weigh peak speed against operability. Try it: serve the same model with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM on one GPU and compare tokens per second at concurrency 1, 16 and 64.

quiz.why: Prefix reuse wins.

quiz.q: llama.cpp and Ollama are best known for…
choices: Running quantized models on CPUs, Macs and small GPUs
quiz.why: They target local and edge inference.

choices: Peak NVIDIA performance at the cost of build/compile steps
quiz.why: Compiled engines are fast but add pipeline work.

lesson.intuition: A serving engine is the software that turns a model file into a fast API: it schedules requests, manages the KV cache, runs optimized kernels and streams tokens. vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, TGI and llama.cpp each make different trade-offs in speed, hardware support and features. Pick for your workload and team, not for a benchmark chart.
how: List requirements: hardware, model families, quantization formats, structured output, multi-LoRA, prefix caching, disaggregation.
Shortlist engines: vLLM and SGLang (open, broad support), TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA-optimized), TGI, llama.cpp/Ollama for CPU and edge.
Benchmark on your traffic shape: input/output lengths, concurrency, SLOs.
Consider operations: upgrades, metrics, community, enterprise support (for example NVIDIA NIM packages).
Plan migration costs: tokenizers, chat templates and tool parsers differ between engines.
lesson.example: Benchmark on your shape: Engine A wins a public benchmark of 128-token prompts. Your workload is 6,000-token RAG prompts with 300-token answers at 50 concurrent users and a p95 TTFT target of 1.5 s. Re-running both engines on that shape, Engine B serves 40% more requests within the SLO because of its prefix caching. Your shape, your results.
mistakes: Choosing an engine from a benchmark with a different input/output length mix.
Forgetting that tool-call and reasoning parsers are engine-specific.
Underestimating the work of upgrading engines that change fast.
lesson.enterprise: A SaaS company runs vLLM for most open models because of broad model support and its OpenAI-compatible API, and uses TensorRT-LLM for one very high-volume model where the extra optimization pays for the engineering effort.
takeaways: Benchmark on your own traffic shape.
Features (prefix cache, LoRA, structured output) often matter more than raw speed.
Count migration and upgrade costs.

subjects.title: GPU Memory Model for Inference
subjects.explainer:
Sizing: parameters times bytes/param plus KV scaling with layers, heads, sequence, batch, precision. PagedAttention treats KV like virtual memory to fight fragmentation.

Common mistake: forgetting KV when estimating 70B fit. Another: huge max_model_len wasting reserved pages.

Back-of-envelope before buying.

topics.title: Fitting

subtopics.title: KV scaling formula
subtopics.text: KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value. GQA lowers the KV head count.

subtopics.title: Fragmentation
subtopics.text: Allocating one big contiguous buffer per request wastes memory when requests end early; paging avoids that.

topics.explainer: GPU memory holds weights, KV cache and activations. Weights are parameters times bytes per parameter: 70B at FP16 is 140 GB. KV per token is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes. Activation peaks happen in prefill of long prompts. Fragmentation wastes memory unless the engine pages it. Engines reserve a fraction of memory up front (for example gpu_memory_utilization 0.9), so nvidia-smi shows "full" even when idle.

topics.title: Techniques

subtopics.title: PagedAttention blocks
subtopics.text: PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size blocks like virtual memory pages, so sequences use only what they need.

subtopics.title: KV quantization
subtopics.text: Storing KV in FP8 halves its size versus bf16, usually with small quality impact; test on your eval.

subtopics.title: Prefix sharing
subtopics.text: Requests sharing a prefix (same system prompt or document) can share its KV blocks.

topics.explainer: PagedAttention stores KV in fixed blocks like virtual memory pages, so there is almost no fragmentation and sequences can share prefix blocks. Quantizing KV to FP8 halves its size. Offloading cold KV to CPU memory or NVMe extends effective capacity at a latency cost. Prefix sharing lets requests with the same system prompt reuse KV. Capping max sequence length per tier is a simple and effective policy for protecting memory.

quiz.why: KV grows with context and concurrency.

quiz.q: Weights of a 70B model in FP16 take about…
quiz.why: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB.

quiz.q: nvidia-smi shows a vLLM GPU "full" at idle because…
choices: The engine pre-reserves memory for KV cache
quiz.why: gpu_memory_utilization reserves space up front.

lesson.intuition: A GPU has a fixed amount of memory and three things compete for it: the model weights, the KV cache for every active sequence, and temporary activations. Weights are fixed; the KV cache grows with every token of every concurrent request. Whether you can serve 5 or 50 users at once is mostly a KV cache question.
how: Weights: parameters × bytes per parameter (2 for bf16, 1 for FP8/INT8, 0.5 for 4-bit).
KV per token: 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes.
KV total: KV per token × tokens per sequence × concurrent sequences.
Leave headroom for activations, CUDA graphs and fragmentation (engines reserve a fraction, e.g. 90%).
Use techniques to fit more: paged KV blocks, KV quantization, prefix sharing, offload and max-length policies.
lesson.example: Fit a 70B model on 2 × 80 GB GPUs: weights in bf16 = 140 GB, leaving ≈ 20 GB minus overhead (say 12 GB) for KV. Llama-3-70B-style KV per token = 2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes ≈ 320 KiB. 12 GB / 320 KiB ≈ 37,000 tokens total, about 4 concurrent 8k-token sequences. In FP8 weights (70 GB), KV room grows to ≈ 80 GB, roughly 250,000 tokens.
mistakes: Sizing only for weights and forgetting the KV cache.
Allowing maximum context for every request, so a few long requests starve everyone.
Ignoring fragmentation, which wastes memory without paged allocation.
lesson.enterprise: A legal search provider capped context at 32k tokens per request for its 70B model and enabled FP8 KV cache, which doubled concurrent users per node without measurable quality loss on their eval.
takeaways: Memory = weights + KV + activations.
KV grows with tokens × concurrency.
Quantize weights and KV to buy batch size.

flowchart LR
  GPU[GPU memory 80 GB] --> W[Weights: fixed]
  GPU --> KV[KV cache: tokens x sequences]
  GPU --> ACT[Activations + overhead]
  KV --> PG[Paged blocks]
  KV --> Q8[FP8 KV]
  KV --> PS[Prefix sharing]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: GPU memory is split between fixed weights, a KV cache that grows with tokens and sequences, and activations; paged blocks, FP8 KV and prefix sharing shrink the KV cost.

subjects.title: Batching, Scheduling & KV Cache
subjects.explainer:
Static batching waits for the slowest. Continuous/in-flight batching lets finished sequences leave. Chunked prefill reduces TTFT interference. Prefix caching and RadixAttention trees, eviction, quantized KV are levers.

Common mistake: maximizing batch until TBT dies. Another: disabling prefix cache on agent workloads.

Plot throughput-latency Pareto curves.

topics.title: Batching

subtopics.title: Static vs continuous
subtopics.text: Static batches run until the longest sequence ends; continuous batching swaps sequences in and out every step.

subtopics.title: Chunked prefill
subtopics.text: Splitting a long prefill into chunks lets decode steps for other users run in between.

subtopics.title: Preemption and priorities
subtopics.text: When KV memory runs out, the scheduler pauses (preempts) some sequences and resumes them later.

topics.explainer: Static batching waits for a full batch and holds GPUs until the longest sequence finishes. Continuous batching adds and removes sequences every step, keeping the GPU busy. Chunked prefill splits long prompts into pieces mixed with decode steps so a big prompt does not freeze everyone's token stream. Schedulers can preempt low-priority requests and enforce fairness between tenants. Knobs such as max batched tokens and max sequences trade latency against throughput.

topics.title: KV Cache

subtopics.title: Prefix caching
subtopics.text: If many requests start with the same tokens, their KV blocks are computed once and reused.

subtopics.title: RadixAttention
subtopics.text: SGLang's RadixAttention stores cached prefixes in a radix tree so partial matches can be reused.

topics.explainer: The KV cache stores keys and values for past tokens so decode does not recompute them. Paged blocks manage it efficiently. Prefix caching reuses KV for identical prompt prefixes across requests; RadixAttention organizes cached prefixes as a tree for automatic matching. When memory fills, the engine evicts least-recently-used blocks or preempts sequences. FP8 or INT8 KV roughly doubles capacity with small quality cost on most models.

choices: Finished leave and new join without waiting for whole batch
quiz.why: In-flight membership raises utilization.

choices: Long prompts from stalling other users' token streams
quiz.why: Splitting prefill lets decode steps interleave.

choices: Many requests share a long system prompt or document
quiz.why: Shared prefixes reuse KV blocks.

lesson.intuition: Because decode reads all weights for every step, serving one request at a time wastes the GPU. Batching runs many requests together so one weight read produces many tokens. Continuous batching goes further: requests join and leave the batch at every step, so short answers don't wait for long ones and the GPU stays busy.
how: Static batching waits for a batch to fill, runs it to completion, and wastes slots when sequences finish early.
Continuous (in-flight) batching adds new requests and removes finished ones every decode step.
Chunked prefill splits long prompts into pieces mixed with decode steps, so one long prompt doesn't stall everyone.
The scheduler decides who runs next, preempts when KV memory runs out, and can apply priorities.
Prefix caching reuses KV blocks for shared prompt beginnings across requests.
lesson.example: Static vs continuous: 4 requests need 10, 50, 50 and 200 output tokens. Static batching runs all 4 for 200 steps: 800 slot-steps, of which only 310 do useful work (39%). Continuous batching frees each slot when its request finishes and fills it from the queue, so with steady demand utilization approaches 100% of slots.
mistakes: Using static batching for chat traffic with very different output lengths.
Letting long prompts block decodes without chunked prefill.
Not enabling prefix caching when every request shares a long system prompt.
lesson.enterprise: A support chatbot with a 3,000-token system prompt enabled prefix caching; prefill work per request dropped by about 80% and p50 TTFT fell from 900 ms to 250 ms.
takeaways: Batching shares the weight read across sequences.
Continuous batching keeps slots full.
Chunked prefill and prefix caching protect latency.

subjects.explainer:

Common mistake: INT4 on safety classifiers. Another: English-only quality checks.

topics.title: Weight Quant

subtopics.title: INT8/4 GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF
subtopics.text: GPTQ and AWQ are post-training methods that quantize weights to 4 bits while minimizing error; GGUF is llama.cpp's format with several bit-widths.

subtopics.title: FP8
subtopics.text: FP8 keeps a floating-point format at 8 bits and is supported natively by recent NVIDIA (Hopper, Blackwell) and AMD GPUs.

subtopics.title: Calibration
subtopics.text: Calibration runs sample inputs through the model to choose good scaling factors.

topics.explainer: Weight quantization stores weights in fewer bits. GPTQ and AWQ produce INT4 weights with small accuracy loss using a calibration set; GGUF is llama.cpp's format with many variants. FP8 on Hopper and newer GPUs keeps quality very close to BF16 with hardware support. Calibrate on data like your traffic. Per-channel or group scales handle outlier columns. Always re-run your evals after quantizing, because averages can hide broken edge cases.

topics.title: Activations & KV

subtopics.title: SmoothQuant ideas
subtopics.text: SmoothQuant moves activation outliers into the weights mathematically, making activations easier to quantize.

subtopics.title: Outliers
subtopics.text: A few very large activation values (outliers) make low-bit quantization lose precision for everything else.

topics.explainer: Activations and KV are harder to quantize than weights because of outliers, a few huge values in certain channels. SmoothQuant shifts that difficulty from activations into weights. KV FP8 is widely supported and usually safe. Symptoms of quantization collapse include repetition, broken formatting and wrong math. Mixed schemes keep sensitive layers in higher precision while quantizing the rest. Try it: enable FP8 KV cache, rerun your eval, and compare both quality and the maximum concurrent sequences the engine reports.

quiz.q: Main serving win from quant is usually…
choices: Higher effective batch from lower memory
quiz.why: Memory→batch→throughput/$.

choices: Hardware support such as Hopper or newer
quiz.why: Native FP8 Tensor Core support makes it fast.

quiz.q: After quantizing a model you must…
quiz.why: Averages can hide broken edge cases.

lesson.intuition: Quantization stores model numbers with fewer bits, like saving a photo at lower quality. Fewer bits per weight means less memory, so you can fit bigger models or more users per GPU, and less data to read per token, so decode gets faster. The risk is accuracy loss, which depends on the method, the model and your task, so always test on your own eval.
how: Choose what to quantize: weights only, weights and activations, and/or the KV cache.
Choose a format: INT8, INT4 (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF variants) or FP8 on hardware that supports it.
Calibrate with a small representative dataset so scales fit real activation ranges.
Evaluate on your task gold set and general benchmarks against the full-precision baseline.
Deploy with an engine that has fast kernels for that format.
lesson.example: Memory and speed: a 70B model in bf16 is 140 GB; in FP8, 70 GB; in 4-bit, about 35 GB plus scales (~38-40 GB). Since decode reads all weights per step, 4-bit weights cut bytes read per token by about 3.5-4× versus bf16, which can greatly speed up single-stream decode if kernels are efficient. Quality must be checked: a 1-point drop may be fine for chat and unacceptable for code.
mistakes: Assuming 4-bit is free; some tasks (math, code, long context) degrade more.
Calibrating on data unlike production traffic.
Using a format the engine can't run fast, losing the speed benefit.
lesson.enterprise: A company serving a 70B model moved from bf16 on 4 GPUs to FP8 on 2 GPUs. On their 1,000-case eval, accuracy dropped 0.3 points, within noise, and cost per million tokens fell by about half.
takeaways: Fewer bits → less memory → more batch → lower cost.
Quality loss is task-specific: always A/B on gold.
Match format to hardware and engine kernels.

topics.title: Methods

subtopics.title: Draft model
subtopics.text: A small model from the same family drafts tokens; it must share the tokenizer with the target.

subtopics.title: EAGLE / Medusa
subtopics.text: Medusa and EAGLE add lightweight heads on the target model that predict several future tokens from its hidden states.

subtopics.title: N-gram lookup
subtopics.text: For edits and code, the next tokens often repeat earlier text, so copying n-grams from the prompt works well.

topics.explainer: Speculative decoding guesses several tokens cheaply and verifies them in one pass of the big model. A small draft model can propose tokens. EAGLE and Medusa add lightweight heads to the target model. N-gram lookup copies spans from the prompt, great for editing and RAG. Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains the model to predict ahead. Tree verification checks several candidate branches at once. Output distribution stays the same as the target model when done correctly.

topics.title: Limits

subtopics.title: Acceptance drivers
subtopics.text: Acceptance is high for predictable text (code, structured output) and lower for creative writing or high temperature.

subtopics.title: Batch collapse
subtopics.text: At large batch sizes the GPU is already compute-bound, so extra verification work can slow things down.

topics.explainer: Speedup depends on acceptance rate: how often the target agrees with the draft. Predictable text (code, templated output) accepts well; creative text less so. At large batch sizes the GPU is already busy, so verification overhead can erase the gain. The draft model costs memory and compute too. Benchmark at your real concurrency and tune the number of speculated tokens.

quiz.why: Memory-bound decode + accepts = wins.

quiz.q: Speculative decoding preserves output quality because…
choices: The target model verifies every accepted token
quiz.why: Rejection sampling keeps the target distribution.

quiz.q: N-gram lookup speculation works especially well for…
choices: Editing and RAG where outputs copy prompt spans
quiz.why: Copied spans are easy to predict from the prompt.

lesson.intuition: Decoding one token at a time leaves a big GPU underused at small batch sizes. Speculative decoding guesses several tokens ahead cheaply, then has the big model check all the guesses in one pass. Correct guesses are kept for free; the first wrong one is replaced. With the standard acceptance rule, the output distribution is exactly what the big model would have produced.
how: A cheap drafter proposes k tokens: a small draft model, extra heads (Medusa, EAGLE), n-gram lookup or built-in multi-token prediction.
The target model scores all k proposals in one forward pass.
Accept tokens left to right while they pass the acceptance test; at the first rejection, sample a corrected token.
Repeat. Speedup depends on acceptance rate and drafter cost.
Turn speculation down or off at large batch sizes, where the GPU is already busy.
lesson.example: Expected tokens per step: with k = 4 draft tokens and per-token acceptance probability α = 0.8, the expected number of tokens produced per target pass is (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α) = (1 − 0.8⁵) / 0.2 = (1 − 0.328) / 0.2 ≈ 3.36. If a target pass plus drafting costs about 1.3× a normal step, speedup ≈ 3.36 / 1.3 ≈ 2.6×.
mistakes: Expecting the same speedup at large batch sizes; there's little idle compute to use.
Using a drafter that predicts your domain poorly, so acceptance is low.
Not checking that implementations preserve output quality (exact or approximate verification).
lesson.enterprise: A code-completion service with low concurrency and highly predictable output enabled n-gram and EAGLE-style speculation and cut median latency per completion by about half; at peak load it automatically reduces draft length.
takeaways: Guess cheaply, verify in one pass.
Acceptance rate drives the speedup.
Best at small batch; tune or disable at high load.

sequenceDiagram

  participant T as Target model
  D->>T: propose t1 t2 t3 t4
  T->>T: one forward pass scores all 4
  T-->>D: accept t1 t2 t3, reject t4
  T-->>D: corrected token t4'
  D->>T: propose next 4
lesson.diagramAlt: Sequence diagram: the drafter proposes four tokens, the target model scores them in one pass, accepts three, rejects the fourth and supplies a corrected token, then drafting continues.

subjects.explainer:
FSM/grammar masking, tool-call parsers, token healing keep outputs valid. Grammar compile cost and cache interactions matter.

Common mistake: regex on unconstrained dumps. Another: recompiling grammars per request.

Validity rate is an SLO.

topics.title: Techniques

subtopics.title: FSM / grammar masking
subtopics.text: The grammar becomes a finite-state machine or pushdown automaton; each state allows only certain next tokens.

subtopics.title: Partial JSON repair
subtopics.text: When streaming, use a tolerant parser to read incomplete JSON safely before the object closes.

subtopics.title: Tool-call parsers
subtopics.text: Engines parse model-specific tool-call formats into structured calls; mismatched parsers cause silent failures.

topics.explainer: Constrained decoding compiles a JSON schema or grammar into a state machine and masks invalid tokens at each step, so output always parses. Token healing fixes boundary issues where the prompt ends mid-token. Partial JSON repair helps clients that parse streams. Tool-call parsers extract function calls from model-specific formats. Version schemas, since changing a schema can change model behavior. Try it: generate 1,000 outputs with and without schema constraints and count parse failures. The difference is usually dramatic.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Compile cost
subtopics.text: Compiling a complex schema takes time; cache compiled grammars and keep schemas reasonably small.

subtopics.title: Failure modes
subtopics.text: Watch for timeouts on complex schemas, truncated JSON at max tokens and grammar compile errors.

subtopics.title: Client contracts
subtopics.text: Document which schema features the server supports so clients don't send ones it rejects.

topics.explainer: Grammar compilation costs time, so cache compiled schemas. Constraints can interact with prefix caching and speculative decoding in engine-specific ways. Failure modes include the model being forced into valid but wrong values, or long loops of whitespace. Agree on contracts with clients about required fields and error handling. Monitor schema violation and repair rates. Try it: log time spent compiling grammars per request; if it is large, cache compiled schemas by hash.

quiz.why: Masked logits implement grammar.

choices: Syntactically valid output for the schema
quiz.why: Valid structure, not necessarily true content.

quiz.q: Grammar compilation cost is best handled by…
quiz.why: Repeated schemas then cost nothing to compile.

lesson.intuition: When an app needs JSON or a tool call, 'please answer in JSON' isn't enough: models sometimes add text or break the format. Constrained decoding enforces the format during generation by masking out any token that would make the output invalid. It guarantees structure, but compiling grammars and masking tokens costs some performance and can interact with caching.
how: Define the output contract as a JSON schema, regex or grammar, versioned with the API.
The engine compiles it into a state machine over tokens.
At each decode step, tokens that would violate the grammar are masked to zero probability.
Parse the result (or partial result when streaming) and validate business rules separately.
Monitor compile time, failure modes and latency overhead.
lesson.example: Masking example: the schema requires {"priority": "low"|"medium"|"high"}. After the model has produced {"priority": ", only tokens that start l, m or h (and continue a valid value) are allowed. If the unconstrained model put 60% probability on "urgent", that mass is removed and the remaining valid tokens are renormalized, so the output parses but you should check whether the forced choice is sensible.
mistakes: Assuming schema-valid means correct; values can still be wrong.
Very large or deeply nested schemas that are slow to compile.
Changing the schema without versioning, breaking clients.
lesson.enterprise: A logistics company extracts shipment events into a strict schema with constrained decoding. Parse failures dropped from 2% to 0%, and a separate validator checks dates and location codes before writing to the database.
takeaways: Constrained decoding guarantees format, not truth.
Version schemas as API contracts.
Watch compile and masking overhead.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SCH[JSON schema] --> COMP[Compile to token FSM]
  COMP --> MASK[Mask invalid tokens each step]
  LLM[Model logits] --> MASK
  MASK --> TOK[Valid token]
  TOK --> OUT[Parseable JSON]
  OUT --> VAL[Business validation]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a JSON schema is compiled to a token state machine that masks invalid tokens from the model's logits at each step, producing parseable JSON that is then validated.

subjects.title: Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
subjects.why: Long prompts stall decodes; split when justified.
subjects.explainer:
Co-located serving couples FTL and TBT. P/D disagg separates pools, transfers KV, rate-matches capacity. Bidirectional KV helps multi-turn.

Common mistake: disaggregating low-ISL chat where co-location wins. Another: ignoring transfer bandwidth.

SLA-aware planners beat static ratios.

topics.title: Motivation

subtopics.title: ISL/OSL asymmetry
subtopics.text: ISL and OSL are input and output sequence lengths. Long inputs with short outputs make prefill dominate.

subtopics.title: Piggyback interference
subtopics.text: When prefill and decode share a GPU, a big prefill delays the next decode step for every active user.

subtopics.title: When co-locate wins
subtopics.text: For short prompts or low traffic, the transfer overhead and extra complexity aren't worth it.

topics.explainer: Prefill is compute-heavy and bursty; decode is memory-bound and steady. On shared GPUs, a large prefill stalls ongoing decodes (interference), hurting time between tokens. Disaggregation runs them on separate GPU pools sized for each phase, so you can match the prefill-to-decode ratio to your input and output lengths. It wins for long inputs and strict latency SLOs; for short prompts and small deployments, co-location is simpler and cheaper.

topics.title: Implementation

subtopics.title: KV transfer
subtopics.text: KV caches can be gigabytes per request; transfer them with RDMA or NVLink to avoid adding latency.

subtopics.title: Proxy orchestration
subtopics.text: A proxy sends each request to a prefill worker, then hands it and its KV cache to a decode worker.

subtopics.title: Capacity planning
subtopics.text: Size prefill and decode pools separately based on prompt lengths and output lengths.

topics.explainer: In a disaggregated setup, a router sends a request to a prefill worker, which computes the KV cache and transfers it to a decode worker over NVLink or RDMA (NIXL, Mooncake and similar libraries do this). The proxy coordinates handoff and streaming. Capacity planning sets the ratio of prefill to decode GPUs. New failure modes include stuck KV transfers and imbalance between pools, so monitor transfer latency and queue depth on both sides.

topics.title: Frameworks & Operations
topics.explainer: Several stacks now ship disaggregated serving: vLLM and SGLang support separate prefill and decode instances with KV connectors, NVIDIA Dynamo adds KV-aware routing and the NIXL transfer library, llm-d brings it to Kubernetes, and Mooncake pioneered a KV-cache-centric design. Operating them means monitoring KV transfer latency and failures, the ratio of prefill to decode capacity, and queueing on each side. Start with co-located serving, measure interference, and move to disaggregation only when TBT SLOs demand it.

subtopics.title: vLLM / SGLang disagg modes
subtopics.text: vLLM and SGLang both offer modes that run prefill and decode on separate workers with KV transfer.

subtopics.title: NVIDIA Dynamo and NIXL
subtopics.text: NVIDIA Dynamo orchestrates disaggregated serving, and NIXL is its library for fast data transfer between GPUs and nodes.

subtopics.title: Monitoring KV transfer
subtopics.text: Monitor KV transfer time and bandwidth, since slow transfers erase the benefit of disaggregation.

choices: Interference between long prefills and ongoing decodes
quiz.why: Stage separation reduces cross-SLO interference.

quiz.q: Co-located prefill and decode is usually better for…
choices: Very long inputs with strict TBT
quiz.why: Disaggregation adds KV transfer and orchestration overhead.

quiz.q: In P/D disaggregation the KV cache is…
choices: Transferred from prefill to decode workers
quiz.why: Transfer over NVLink/RDMA avoids recomputation.

lesson.intuition: Prefill (reading the prompt) and decode (writing the answer) want different things: prefill wants lots of compute in bursts, decode wants steady memory bandwidth and low latency. Running both on the same GPUs means long prompts interrupt everyone's token stream. Disaggregation puts them on separate GPU pools and ships the KV cache between them.
how: Measure your traffic: input and output lengths and their ratio, plus TTFT and ITL targets.
Run prefill workers that process prompts and produce KV caches.
Transfer KV to decode workers over fast interconnects (NVLink, RDMA via libraries like NIXL).
Decode workers generate tokens with stable inter-token latency.
Size each pool separately to its SLO, and fall back to co-location when it's cheaper.
lesson.example: Pool sizing: 20 requests per second with 4,000 input and 300 output tokens. If a prefill GPU handles 40,000 prompt tokens per second, prefill needs 20 × 4,000 / 40,000 = 2 GPUs (plus headroom, say 3). If a decode GPU sustains 3,000 output tokens per second at the target ITL, decode needs 20 × 300 / 3,000 = 2 GPUs (say 3). The ratio comes from your traffic, not a fixed rule.
mistakes: Disaggregating short-prompt workloads where co-location is simpler and cheaper.
Ignoring KV transfer bandwidth and its latency.
Fixed prefill:decode ratios that don't track traffic changes.
lesson.enterprise: A document-QA service with 30k-token prompts saw ITL spikes whenever a long prompt arrived. Splitting prefill and decode pools stabilized p99 ITL and let them scale prefill GPUs separately during morning document uploads.
takeaways: Split when long prompts hurt decode latency.
KV transfer speed makes or breaks it.
Size pools from your traffic and SLOs.

flowchart LR
  R[Requests] --> RT[Router / proxy]
  RT --> PF[Prefill pool]
  PF -->|KV transfer: NVLink / RDMA| DC[Decode pool]
  DC --> S[Stream tokens]

Common mistake: TP across nodes without bandwidth. Another: EP without load-balance monitors.

NCCL tests are bring-up.

topics.title: Types

subtopics.title: Tensor parallel
subtopics.text: Each GPU holds a slice of every weight matrix; results are combined with all-reduce after each layer.

subtopics.title: Pipeline parallel
subtopics.text: Layers are split into stages; micro-batches flow through the pipeline so stages work in parallel.

subtopics.title: Expert parallel
subtopics.text: Each GPU holds some experts, and tokens are sent to whichever GPU holds their chosen experts.

topics.explainer: When a model does not fit on one GPU, split it. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs and needs fast all-reduce, so keep it within an NVLink domain. Pipeline parallelism assigns layers to stages, tolerating slower links but adding bubbles. Expert parallelism places MoE experts on different GPUs with all-to-all routing. Sequence or context parallelism splits very long sequences. Large deployments combine them.

topics.title: Communication

subtopics.title: NCCL collectives
subtopics.text: NCCL provides all-reduce, all-gather and all-to-all collectives optimized for NVIDIA GPUs and networks.

subtopics.title: Topology awareness
subtopics.text: Place communicating GPUs on the fastest links (same NVLink domain, same switch).

topics.explainer: Distributed inference lives or dies on communication. NCCL provides collectives such as all-reduce and all-to-all. NVLink and NVSwitch give hundreds of GB/s inside a node or rack; InfiniBand or RoCE connect nodes at lower bandwidth. Good engines overlap communication with compute. Place tensor-parallel groups inside the fastest domain and check the topology with nvidia-smi topo -m before blaming the model.

choices: Matmuls across GPUs for one replica
quiz.why: TP splits layer math.

quiz.q: Pipeline parallelism tolerates slower links but adds…
quiz.why: Stages idle while waiting for micro-batches.

quiz.q: Expert parallelism mainly generates which collective?
quiz.why: Tokens are dispatched to experts on other GPUs and gathered back.

lesson.intuition: When a model is too big for one GPU, or too slow on one, you split it. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs; pipeline parallelism gives each GPU a slice of layers; expert parallelism spreads MoE experts across GPUs. Each split needs GPUs to talk, so the network (NVLink, InfiniBand) becomes part of the model's speed.
how: Tensor parallel (TP): split matrices across GPUs, with all-reduce communication every layer. Best inside a node over NVLink.
Pipeline parallel (PP): split layers into stages across GPUs or nodes; pass activations between stages.
Expert parallel (EP): place different MoE experts on different GPUs; route tokens with all-to-all communication.
Sequence/context parallel: split very long sequences across GPUs.
Combine them (e.g. TP within a node, PP across nodes) based on topology, and test collectives with NCCL tests.
lesson.example: TP communication: with TP = 8 and hidden size 8,192, each layer does two all-reduces of activations of size tokens × 8,192 × 2 bytes. For a decode batch of 64 tokens, that's 64 × 8,192 × 2 = 1 MiB per all-reduce, small enough that NVLink latency, not bandwidth, dominates. That's why TP across nodes over slower links usually hurts.
mistakes: Using tensor parallelism across nodes over slow networks.
Ignoring GPU topology, so communication crosses slow links.
Skipping NCCL bandwidth tests during bring-up.
lesson.enterprise: A team serving a 400B-class MoE model uses TP = 8 inside each 8-GPU node and expert parallelism across 4 nodes over InfiniBand, after NCCL tests showed one node with a faulty link that halved all-to-all bandwidth.
takeaways: TP inside the node, PP or EP across nodes.
Communication is part of model speed.
Test the fabric before blaming the model.

    G2 --- G3[GPU ...8]

subjects.explainer:
Multi-LoRA batching hosts many adapters with request routing. Memory, hot-swap, noisy-neighbor need policy.

Common mistake: thousands of cold adapters in GPU memory. Another: no tenant rate isolation.

Adapters are first-class deployables.

topics.title: Memory & Routing

subtopics.title: Adapter footprints
subtopics.text: Adapters are usually tens of megabytes, versus gigabytes for the base model.

subtopics.title: Request routing
subtopics.text: Send requests to replicas that already have their adapter loaded to avoid load delays.

subtopics.title: Batching constraints
subtopics.text: Batching sequences with different adapters needs special kernels; adapters of different ranks may batch less efficiently.

topics.explainer: Multi-LoRA serving keeps one base model in memory and loads many small adapters. Adapters are megabytes to hundreds of megabytes each. The router sends each request to a server that has its adapter loaded; hot adapters stay in GPU memory, cold ones live in CPU or disk. Kernels such as Punica and S-LoRA batch requests with different adapters together. Quantized adapters save more memory.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Versioning
subtopics.text: Version each adapter and record which base model it was trained for.

subtopics.title: Canary
subtopics.text: Roll out a new adapter version to a small share of that customer's traffic and compare evals before switching fully.

subtopics.title: Noisy neighbor
subtopics.text: One busy adapter's traffic can slow others sharing the GPU; use per-adapter limits.

topics.explainer: Treat adapters as deployable artifacts with versions. Canary new adapters on a slice of traffic. A heavily used adapter can starve others, so enforce fairness. Keep rollback instant by retaining the previous version. Emit metrics per adapter (latency, errors, quality) so tenant-specific problems are visible. A useful rule: an adapter is a release, not a file. Give it a version, an owner, an eval report and a rollback path. Try it: serve two adapters on one base model and route by request header, watching latency per adapter.

choices: Host many adapters on one base engine
quiz.why: Specialization without full replicas.

choices: One base model plus many small adapters
quiz.why: Adapters share the base weights.

choices: CPU memory or disk until requested
quiz.why: Hot ones are promoted to GPU memory.

lesson.intuition: Many customers want their own fine-tuned model, but running a full copy for each is too expensive. LoRA adapters are tiny add-ons to a shared base model, so one GPU can serve hundreds of 'different' models by loading the right adapter for each request. The challenge is memory, routing and batching requests that use different adapters together.
how: Keep one base model in GPU memory and many small LoRA adapters in GPU, CPU or storage.
Route each request to a replica that has its adapter loaded (or can load it fast).
Batch requests across adapters using kernels that apply different adapters per sequence (e.g. S-LoRA/Punica-style).
Keep hot adapters in GPU memory, warm ones in CPU memory, and cold ones on disk.
Version, canary and monitor each adapter separately.
lesson.example: Adapter size: a rank-16 LoRA on the 4 attention projections of a 32-layer, 4,096-hidden model has about 16.8M parameters; in bf16 that's ≈ 34 MB. A GPU with 10 GB spare could hold about 300 such adapters, compared with one extra full 16 GB copy of the 8B base model.
mistakes: Pinning each customer to a dedicated GPU instead of sharing the base.
Random routing that loads and unloads adapters constantly.
No per-adapter metrics, so one customer's bad adapter goes unnoticed.
lesson.enterprise: A customer-support platform serves 600 customer-specific adapters on a shared 8B base. Adapter-aware routing keeps each customer's adapter on two replicas, and per-adapter evals gate every new version.
takeaways: One base, many tiny adapters.
Route by adapter to avoid thrashing.
Treat each adapter as a release.

flowchart LR
  R1[Req: customer A] --> RT[Adapter-aware router]
  R2[Req: customer B] --> RT
  RT --> REP[Replica: base model]
  REP --- AA[Adapter A: GPU]
  REP --- AB[Adapter B: GPU]
  CPU[(Warm adapters: CPU)] -.load.-> REP
  DISK[(Cold adapters: disk)] -.load.-> CPU

subjects.title: Weight Loading & Cold Start
subjects.why: Autoscaling LLMs fails if a new replica takes ten minutes to become ready.
subjects.explainer:
A new replica must get a node, pull an image, load tens to hundreds of GB of weights, initialize the engine and warm up. Each step can be measured and shortened. This subject covers where time goes, fast loading techniques, and how to choose between always-on, warm pools and scale-to-zero per model.

Common mistakes: pulling weights from object storage on every start; huge images with weights baked in and no layer caching; autoscaling on signals that react too late for a minutes-long cold start.

subjects.project: Measure each cold-start phase for a 7B-70B model: node ready, image pull, weight load (object store vs local NVMe vs streamer), engine init, first token. Then cut total time by at least half and document which change mattered most.

topics.title: Where the Time Goes
topics.explainer: Break cold start into phases and time each: node provisioning (cloud can take minutes), image pull (CUDA images are often 10+ GB), weight download and load into GPU memory (model bytes ÷ bandwidth), engine initialization (KV cache allocation, CUDA graph capture, kernel compilation such as torch.compile), and warmup requests. Without measurement, teams optimize the wrong phase. Log timestamps for each phase on every start and keep the distribution, not just one run.

subtopics.title: Weight transfer and load
subtopics.text: Weights for large models are tens to hundreds of gigabytes; download speed often dominates cold start.

subtopics.title: Engine init and CUDA graphs
subtopics.text: Engines capture CUDA graphs and run warmup requests, which can take a minute or more.

topics.title: Fast Loading Techniques
topics.explainer: Shorten the big phases. Keep weights on node-local NVMe or a shared high-throughput cache rather than object storage. Use safetensors so tensors can be memory-mapped and streamed. Stream tensors concurrently straight to GPU memory. Pre-shard checkpoints to your tensor-parallel layout so each GPU reads only its slice. Keep images slim and pre-pulled on nodes; use lazy-loading image formats. Cache compiled artifacts (CUDA graphs, compile caches) where your engine supports it.

subtopics.title: Local NVMe and caches
subtopics.text: Cache model weights on local NVMe so new replicas don't download them over the network.

subtopics.title: safetensors and mmap
subtopics.text: safetensors files can be memory-mapped and loaded quickly and safely, unlike pickle-based formats.

subtopics.title: Image slimming and pre-pull
subtopics.text: Smaller container images and pre-pulling them onto nodes cut startup time.

topics.title: Scale-to-Zero vs Warm Pools
topics.explainer: Every model needs a readiness policy. Hot models stay always-on with headroom. Warm models keep a small pool of ready replicas and scale out from there. Cold models scale to zero and accept a first-request delay, shown honestly in the UI. Scale on leading signals (queue depth, request rate trends) and pre-scale for known peaks. For multi-model platforms, multiplex many rarely used models or LoRA adapters on shared replicas instead of dedicating GPUs to each.

subtopics.title: Hot / warm / cold tiers
subtopics.text: Hot replicas serve now, warm ones have weights cached and start fast, cold ones start from scratch.

subtopics.title: Leading autoscale signals
subtopics.text: Queue depth and request rate rise before GPU utilization does, so scale on them.

quiz.q: Time to load 140 GB of weights at 7 GB/s is about…
quiz.why: 140 ÷ 7 = 20 seconds.

quiz.q: Pre-sharding checkpoints to the TP layout helps because…
choices: Each GPU reads only its slice
quiz.why: Less data per GPU, loaded in parallel.

quiz.q: Scale-to-zero is a good fit for…
choices: Rarely used models where a first-request delay is acceptable
quiz.why: Savings outweigh occasional cold starts.

quiz.q: Why is safetensors faster to load than pickle checkpoints?
choices: It can be memory-mapped without code execution
quiz.why: Raw tensor layout enables zero-copy mapping.

lesson.intuition: Autoscaling a normal web service takes seconds. A new LLM replica can take many minutes: get a GPU node, pull a large container, copy tens of gigabytes of weights, load them onto the GPU and warm up the engine. If you only scale when the queue is already long, users wait. Cold-start work shrinks each phase and keeps some capacity warm.
how: Time each phase: node provisioning, image pull, weight download, load to GPU, engine init (CUDA graphs, warmup).
Cut image size and pre-pull images on GPU nodes.
Cache weights on local NVMe or a fast shared store; use safetensors with memory mapping and parallel streaming to GPU.
Keep warm pools or scale-to-zero only for low-priority models; scale on leading signals (queue depth, request rate) and schedules.
Show users a loading state when a cold model must start.
lesson.example: Phase budget: node 180 s + image pull 120 s + 140 GB weights at 1 GB/s from object storage 140 s + GPU load 40 s + init 60 s = 540 s (9 minutes). With pre-pulled images (0 s), weights on local NVMe at 5 GB/s (28 s) and a warm node pool (0 s), it's 28 + 40 + 60 ≈ 128 s, about 2 minutes.
mistakes: Measuring only total startup time, not each phase.
Autoscaling on GPU utilization, which reacts too late.
Huge container images that bundle weights and tools nobody uses.
lesson.enterprise: An AI search company keeps one warm replica per popular model, pre-scales before known daily peaks, and caches weights on node-local NVMe. New replicas are ready in under 2 minutes instead of 10, and peak queue times dropped sharply.
takeaways: Measure every startup phase.
Move weights close to the GPU and load in parallel.
Scale on leading signals and keep a warm pool.

subjects.title: LLM Gateways & Inference Routing
subjects.why: Routing decides cost, latency and resilience before a single token is generated.
subjects.explainer:
Gateways give every app one endpoint with keys, budgets, policy and traces, and route across providers, models and replicas. Inside a self-hosted fleet, KV- and prefix-aware routing can cut prefill work dramatically. This subject covers gateway functions, endpoint picking, and multi-model policies.

Common mistakes: round-robin across LLM replicas; fallbacks to models never evaluated with your prompts; gateways without per-tenant budgets.

topics.title: Gateway Functions
topics.explainer: A production gateway terminates auth, maps virtual keys to provider keys, enforces rate limits and budgets per team, normalizes request formats, runs policy hooks (PII redaction, injection screening, content rules), applies retries, fallbacks and hedging, and emits traces with tokens and cost. It is also where you implement model aliases ('support-default' points to a specific model version) so apps never hard-code model names.

subtopics.title: Virtual keys and budgets
subtopics.text: Virtual keys map to teams or apps, each with its own budget and allowed models, without sharing provider keys.

subtopics.title: Retries, fallbacks, hedging
subtopics.text: Retries handle transient errors, fallbacks switch models or providers, and hedging sends duplicates to cut tail latency.

topics.title: KV- and Prefix-Aware Routing
topics.explainer: LLM replicas are stateful: each holds a KV cache. A smart endpoint picker scores replicas on queue length, KV utilization, loaded LoRA adapters and prefix-cache affinity, sending requests that share a prefix to the replica that already cached it. This avoids recomputing long system prompts and documents. Balance affinity with load to avoid hot spots. The Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension standardizes this pattern; llm-d and Dynamo implement it with cache-aware schedulers.

subtopics.title: Why round-robin fails
subtopics.text: Round-robin ignores how busy each replica is and where cached prefixes live.

subtopics.title: Prefix-cache affinity
subtopics.text: Send requests with the same prefix to the same replica so its KV cache can be reused.

topics.title: Multi-Model & Multi-Provider Policy
topics.explainer: Routing policy decides which model serves a request: by tier, task, cost budget, region or a learned difficulty score. Fallback chains handle provider outages and rate limits. Every target in a chain must be evaluated with your prompts, or failover silently lowers quality. Log the routing decision with each request so cost and quality can be attributed. Review policies regularly as prices and models change.

subtopics.title: Tier and task routing
subtopics.text: Send each request to a model tier based on task type and customer tier.

subtopics.title: Fallback chains
subtopics.text: If the first model fails or is overloaded, try a predefined list of alternatives.

subtopics.title: Eval parity for fallbacks
subtopics.text: Run the same eval on primary and fallback models so you know how much quality drops during a failover.

topics.title: Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension and llm-d
topics.explainer: The Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension adds model-aware routing to standard gateways: an InferencePool groups model-server pods, and an endpoint picker chooses a pod using live signals such as queue depth, KV-cache utilization and loaded LoRA adapters. llm-d builds on vLLM and this extension for distributed inference on Kubernetes, adding prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV cache offloading. Databricks AI Gateway and similar products provide the higher-level policy layer.

subtopics.title: InferencePool and endpoint picker
subtopics.text: An InferencePool groups model-server pods; the endpoint picker chooses one per request using live metrics.

subtopics.title: Queue- and KV-aware scheduling
subtopics.text: Route requests to the replica with the shortest queue or the most reusable KV cache.

subtopics.title: Policy gateways (Databricks AI Gateway) vs inference routers
subtopics.text: Policy gateways handle auth, budgets and logging; inference routers optimize placement on replicas.

choices: Prefill compute for shared prompt prefixes
quiz.why: Cached KV for the prefix is reused.

quiz.q: Model aliases in a gateway let you…
choices: Swap the underlying model without app changes
quiz.why: Apps call a stable name.

quiz.q: A fallback model that was never evaluated with your prompts risks…
quiz.why: Prompts tuned for one model may fail on another.

quiz.q: Why is round-robin a poor fit for LLM replicas?
choices: It ignores KV state, queue depth and cached prefixes
quiz.why: Replicas are stateful and unevenly loaded.

lesson.intuition: An inference gateway decides where every request goes before a single token is generated. At the business level it routes between providers and models with keys, budgets and fallbacks. At the cluster level it picks the replica that will answer fastest, using signals like queue length, free KV cache, cached prefixes and loaded LoRA adapters. Round-robin ignores all of that.
how: Normalize request formats and authenticate with virtual keys tied to budgets.
Apply policy: allowed models per team, PII hooks, model aliases.
Choose model and provider by tier and task, with fallback chains that have similar eval quality.
Inside the cluster, score replicas on queue depth, KV utilization, prefix-cache match and adapter availability.
Log every routing decision for debugging and policy review.
lesson.example: Prefix-aware routing: 4 replicas serve 200 customers, each with a 6,000-token prefix (its documents and instructions). With round-robin, every replica must hold every prefix: 200 × 6,000 = 1.2M tokens of KV per replica, more than fits (say 400,000 tokens), so prefixes are evicted and recomputed constantly. Routing each customer to one home replica means each replica holds only about 50 prefixes (300,000 tokens), which fits, so most requests skip most of their prefill. Hot customers are spread across two replicas to avoid hot spots.
mistakes: Round-robin balancing that destroys cache locality.
Fallback models never evaluated against the primary.
No logs of why a request went where it did.
lesson.enterprise: A platform running llm-d on Kubernetes uses the Gateway API Inference Extension so an endpoint picker chooses pods based on queue depth and KV-cache state. Under the same load, p95 TTFT dropped about 40% compared with plain round-robin.
takeaways: Route on real-time engine signals, not round-robin.
Fallbacks need eval parity.
Log routing decisions.

topics.title: Attention Kernels

subtopics.title: FlashAttention IO awareness
subtopics.text: FlashAttention reorders the attention computation to minimize reads and writes to GPU main memory.

subtopics.title: MLA variants
subtopics.text: Multi-head latent attention (used in DeepSeek models) compresses keys and values into a smaller latent, needing specialized kernels.

topics.explainer: FlashAttention computes attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip SRAM, avoiding writing the huge score matrix to HBM; it is exact, just IO-aware. GQA and MQA kernels exploit shared KV heads. Paged attention kernels read KV from scattered blocks. MLA variants decompress latent KV on the fly. Numeric modes (BF16, FP8) change speed and accuracy, and newer GPUs add special instructions for them.

topics.title: Tooling

subtopics.title: Triton
subtopics.text: Triton is a Python-like language for writing GPU kernels without raw CUDA.

subtopics.title: CUDA graphs
subtopics.text: CUDA graphs record a sequence of kernel launches once and replay it, removing CPU launch overhead.

subtopics.title: Roofline
subtopics.text: A roofline plot shows whether a kernel is limited by compute or memory bandwidth, telling you what to optimize.

topics.explainer: Profile before optimizing. Nsight Systems shows the timeline of kernels, copies and gaps; Nsight Compute digs into one kernel. Triton lets you write custom GPU kernels in Python. CUDA graphs remove CPU launch overhead, which matters a lot in decode. torch.compile fuses operations automatically. The roofline model tells you whether a kernel is limited by compute or memory bandwidth, and therefore which optimization can help.

quiz.why: IO-aware tiling cuts HBM trips.
Replaying captured graphs avoids per-kernel launch cost, important in decode.

quiz.q: The roofline model tells you whether a kernel is…
quiz.why: That decides which optimizations can help.

lesson.intuition: A kernel is a small program that runs on the GPU, such as one matrix multiply or one attention step. Most LLM speedups come from better kernels that move less data between slow and fast memory. FlashAttention is the famous example: it computes exact attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory instead of writing a huge score matrix to slow memory.
how: Profile first (Nsight Systems/Compute, PyTorch profiler) to see which kernels take the time.
Use a roofline view: is the kernel limited by compute or by memory bandwidth?
Use optimized implementations: FlashAttention, paged attention kernels, fused ops.
Reduce launch overhead with CUDA graphs and torch.compile.
Write custom kernels (e.g. in Triton) only when profiling shows a clear win.
lesson.example: Why FlashAttention helps: for one head with sequence length 8,192, the full attention score matrix has 8,192² ≈ 67M entries; in fp16 that's ≈ 134 MB written and read per head per layer. FlashAttention never stores it, processing tiles in on-chip SRAM and keeping running softmax statistics, so memory traffic grows roughly linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, while computing the same result.
mistakes: Optimizing kernels before profiling.
Comparing kernels at batch sizes or sequence lengths you don't use.
Ignoring numeric differences between precision modes.
lesson.enterprise: An inference team found that 15% of decode time went to small elementwise kernels. Fusing them and capturing CUDA graphs cut per-token latency by 12% without changing the model.
takeaways: Profile, then optimize.
Memory movement is usually the bottleneck.
FlashAttention: exact attention, tiled, no big score matrix.

flowchart LR
  HBM[(HBM: large, slow)] -->|load tile Q, K, V| SRAM[On-chip SRAM: small, fast]
  SRAM --> COMP[Scores + online softmax]
  COMP --> ACC[Accumulate output]
  ACC -->|write output only| HBM
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: FlashAttention loads tiles of Q, K and V from slow HBM into fast on-chip SRAM, computes scores with online softmax, accumulates output and writes only the output back.

subjects.explainer:
Load shapes, concurrency vs batch, autoscale signals, warm pools, admission control, shedding, fallbacks, priority lanes.

Common mistake: autoscaling on CPU while GPUs bottleneck. Another: no overload playbook.

Write runbooks while calm.

topics.title: Planning

subtopics.title: Load shapes
subtopics.text: Look at daily and weekly patterns, bursts and prompt-length mix, not just average requests per second.

subtopics.title: Concurrency vs batch
subtopics.text: Concurrency is requests in flight; each replica has a maximum before latency targets break.

subtopics.title: Headroom
subtopics.text: Keep spare capacity for spikes and failures, because GPUs can't be added in seconds.

topics.explainer: Capacity planning starts with load shape: requests per second, input and output lengths, and how bursty traffic is. Concurrency is not batch size; many concurrent users can be served by continuous batching on few GPUs until KV memory runs out. Autoscale on queue depth or tokens in flight, not CPU. Keep warm pools because cold starts on GPUs take minutes. Hold headroom for spikes and failures.

topics.title: Degradation

subtopics.title: Admission control
subtopics.text: Reject or queue new requests when the system is full, instead of letting everyone slow down.

subtopics.title: Priority lanes
subtopics.text: Give critical or paying traffic its own queue so it isn't stuck behind bulk jobs.

topics.explainer: When demand exceeds capacity, degrade on purpose. Admission control rejects or queues requests before they hurt everyone. Shed non-critical traffic such as batch jobs first. Fall back to a smaller model for some tiers. Use priority lanes so paying or interactive users keep their SLOs. Communicate clearly during incidents, including status pages, because silent slowness erodes trust faster than an honest message.

quiz.why: SLO-compliant useful work.

choices: Queue depth or tokens in flight
quiz.why: CPU barely moves when GPUs saturate.

choices: GPU cold starts (node + image + weights) take minutes
quiz.why: Spikes cannot wait for cold capacity.

lesson.intuition: Inference capacity planning is site reliability engineering with expensive, slow-to-scale GPUs. You need to know your traffic shape, how many concurrent requests one replica can serve within your latency targets, and what you'll do when demand exceeds supply: queue, shed, downgrade or prioritize. Plan for peaks, not averages.
how: Characterize load: requests per second over the day, input/output lengths, burstiness.
Benchmark one replica: the maximum concurrency that still meets TTFT and ITL targets (goodput).
Size replicas for peak plus headroom, and set autoscaling on leading signals with warm pools.
Define degradation: admission control, priority lanes, shedding non-critical traffic, fallback models.
Prepare incident communications and practice them.
lesson.example: Little's law sizing: peak 30 requests per second, each lasting 8 s on average (prefill + 400 tokens decode), means 30 × 8 = 240 concurrent requests. If one replica meets SLOs up to 40 concurrent requests, you need 6 replicas, plus 30% headroom ≈ 8 replicas at peak.
mistakes: Sizing for average load instead of peak.
Scaling on GPU utilization, which stays high even when latency is fine or bad.
No plan for what to shed when demand exceeds capacity.
lesson.enterprise: A tax-software company plans for a peak 10× normal traffic in the last week before the filing deadline. It pre-scales by date, reserves a priority lane for paying users, and switches free users to a smaller model when queues exceed 2 seconds.
takeaways: Concurrency = arrival rate × duration.
Plan for peak with headroom.
Decide degradation before the incident.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  LOAD[Load shape] --> BENCH[Per-replica goodput]
  BENCH --> SIZE[Replicas = peak concurrency / per-replica + headroom]
  SIZE --> AS[Autoscale + warm pool]
  AS --> DEG{Over capacity?}
  DEG -->|yes| ADM[Admission control, priority lanes, fallback model]
  DEG -->|no| OK[Serve]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: load shape and per-replica goodput give a replica count with headroom, autoscaling with a warm pool, and admission control, priority lanes and fallback models when over capacity.

topics.explainer: Hardware sets serving economics. NVIDIA Blackwell and GB200 NVL72 racks connect 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, ideal for big MoE models. AMD Instinct GPUs with ROCm offer large HBM and are supported by major engines. CPU-plus-GPU superchips share memory coherently. Other accelerators (TPUs, Trainium, Gaudi, inference ASICs) can be cheaper for supported models. Power per rack is now a first-class constraint.

topics.title: Memory

subtopics.title: HBM capacity/bandwidth
subtopics.text: HBM capacity limits model and KV size per GPU; bandwidth limits decode speed.

subtopics.title: CXL pools
subtopics.text: CXL lets servers attach extra memory over a PCIe-based link, a possible tier for KV caches.

topics.explainer: HBM capacity decides how many sequences and how much context fit; HBM bandwidth decides decode speed. KV offload to CPU or NVMe and CXL memory pools extend capacity. Multi-host KV stores let any server reuse cached prefixes. Each extra tier adds latency and new failure domains, so measure hit rates before adding complexity. Try it: compute how many 8k-token sequences fit in the KV budget of your GPU, then compare with what the engine logs at startup.

quiz.why: Collectives demand fabric.
Decode re-reads weights each step.

quiz.q: A GB200 NVL72 rack is notable for…
quiz.why: Large NVLink domains suit big TP and MoE.

lesson.intuition: Hardware sets the limits for inference: how much memory each accelerator has, how fast it can read that memory, how many accelerators can talk at high speed, and how much power the rack can deliver. Newer systems like NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 connect 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, and memory tiers like CPU memory and CXL change how big KV caches can get.
how: Compare accelerators on HBM capacity, memory bandwidth, low-precision compute (FP8/FP4) and interconnect.
Consider software maturity: CUDA, ROCm for AMD, and support for other accelerators in your engine.
Plan memory tiers: HBM for hot data, CPU memory or NVMe for KV offload, emerging CXL pools.
Check power and cooling: rack density can require liquid cooling.
Define failure domains: what happens when one GPU in a large NVLink domain fails.
lesson.example: Bandwidth bound on decode: a 70B model in FP8 is 70 GB. On an accelerator with 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth (Blackwell-class B200 is about 8 TB/s), a single sequence can decode at most ≈ 8,000 / 70 ≈ 114 tokens per second; on 3.35 TB/s (H100), ≈ 48 tokens per second. More bandwidth directly raises single-stream speed.
mistakes: Comparing peak FLOPs while your workload is memory-bandwidth-bound.
Ignoring software support for non-NVIDIA hardware.
Ordering high-density racks without the power and cooling to run them.
lesson.enterprise: A cloud provider tests AMD MI300X for a 70B model because its 192 GB of HBM fits the model and a large KV cache on one GPU, avoiding tensor parallelism, after confirming vLLM support on ROCm for their models.
takeaways: Memory capacity and bandwidth drive inference.
Software support is part of the hardware choice.
Power and cooling are hard limits.

Before adopting a paper, check whether the gains hold at your batch sizes, models and hardware, and whether a maintained engine already implements it.

choices: Confirm it targets your measured bottleneck
quiz.why: Bottleneck fit first.

quiz.q: A paper's speedup may not transfer if…
choices: Your batch sizes, models or hardware differ
quiz.why: Gains are often regime-specific.

choices: Output length or cost of requests
quiz.why: Better length estimates improve batching and fairness.

lesson.intuition: Inference research moves into production engines within months: PagedAttention, FlashAttention, speculative decoding and disaggregation all started as papers. A watchlist helps you notice ideas that matter for your workload, read them critically and test them, without chasing every new preprint.
how: Follow a few sources: engine release notes (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM), major conferences (MLSys, OSDI, NeurIPS) and arXiv.
For each idea, ask: which bottleneck does it attack (compute, memory, communication, scheduling)? Does my workload have it?
Check the evaluation setup: model sizes, sequence lengths, batch sizes and hardware.
Reproduce on your traffic shape before adopting.
Track adoption: when an engine ships it, test it behind a flag.
lesson.example: Reading a claim critically: a paper reports '3× throughput'. The fine print: batch size 1, 128-token outputs, a 7B model on one GPU. Your workload is batch 64 with 1,000-token outputs on a 70B model with TP = 4. Speculative-style gains usually shrink at large batch, so expect much less and measure before planning capacity around it.
mistakes: Adopting a technique because of a headline number from a different workload.
Ignoring engine release notes, where features land first.
Testing new features without a flag and a rollback.
lesson.enterprise: An inference team reviews new papers monthly in a 30-minute session, keeps a table of ideas mapped to bottlenecks, and runs a benchmark whenever a relevant feature lands in their engine. Prefix-aware routing and FP8 KV both went from 'watch' to production this way.
takeaways: Map each idea to a bottleneck.
Check the evaluation setup against yours.
Adopt behind flags, with benchmarks.

  FIT -->|no| WATCH[Watchlist]
  FIT -->|yes| REPRO[Reproduce on my traffic]
  REPRO --> FLAG[Ship behind flag]
  FLAG --> PROD[Production]
